summary: This one-page industry handout, dated January 2018, defends neonicotinoid seed treatments as valuable tools in integrated pest management and describes industry efforts to make them safer for pollinators and wildlife. It cites an AgInfomatics economic analysis of yield benefits, outlines bee health partnerships, and gives stewardship practices for handling, planting and disposing of treated seed to limit dust-off and pesticide exposure.
one_line: Industry handout (January 2018) promoting neonicotinoid seed treatments and describing stewardship practices to protect pollinators and wildlife.
key_facts: Neonicotinoids provide a unique mode of action that is necessary to manage pests resistant to other insecticides.

An AgInfomatics economic analysis of more than 1,500 field studies conducted over 20 years found neonicotinoid insecticides provided average yield increases ranging from 3.6 percent to 71.3 percent in eight major crops across North America.
The handout states the average yield benefit of using neonicotinoids far exceeds the cost of treatment and delivers a substantial economic return on investment to the farmer.

The crop protection and seed industries are partnering with other organizations in the Honey Bee Health Coalition to improve pollinator habitat and forage, create hive management tools, and develop strategies to control crop pests while safeguarding pollinator health.
Farmers and beekeepers depend on each other where bees are needed to pollinate crops; the farmer gets greater crop productivity and the beekeeper earns a fee for pollination.

Seed treatments give farmers an economical means of protecting seeds and seedlings against early-season insect pests and diseases, resulting in stronger and more uniform stands and higher crop yields.
Seed treatments, including those with neonicotinoid pesticides, undergo rigorous testing and review by the EPA before being permitted for commercial use.

Industry improvements include enhancing seed coating polymers and application processes to reduce dust-off, developing new flow agents for planting equipment, and implementing an ISO planting equipment standard to better control dust emissions.
Stewardship guidance says to follow directions on treated seed container labeling for handling, storage, planting and disposal.
Spilled seeds should be removed or covered by soil to protect wildlife and the environment.
At planting, users should be aware of honey bees and hives near the field and communicate with beekeepers when possible.
Flowering plants and weeds in and around the field should be eliminated prior to planting.
Treated seed left in containers and equipment used to handle harvested grain must be completely removed and disposed of properly, and kept out of commodity grain channels.
Users should use advanced seed flow lubricants that minimize dust.
More detailed stewardship information is available at seed-treatment-guide.com.
